parts.title: 大問1 短文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 1〜2文・会話の空所に入る単語・句動詞を4つから選ぶ（準1級の語彙）
parts.tip: まず空所の後ろの2文目や because / but / despite を見て「良い意味か悪い意味か」を決める。次に前置詞（convert A into B, susceptible to）で形を絞る。句動詞は動詞より後ろの小さい語（down / out / up）の意味をつかむ。
parts.intro: Read each sentence or short exchange and choose the word or phrase that best fills the blank.

questions.q: The committee voted to ____ the outdated rule after several members complained that it no longer served any useful purpose and only slowed down decision-making.
choices: inhabit
endorse
provoke
abolish
questions.why: abolish＝「（制度・規則を）廃止する」。役に立たず決定を遅らせるだけ、という理由に合う。inhabit（住む）、endorse（支持する）、provoke（引き起こす）は理由と合わない。

questions.q: Despite the ____ weather forecast, thousands of fans gathered in the park for the outdoor concert, and fortunately the rain held off until the final song.
choices: lavish
gloomy
fragile
vacant
questions.why: gloomy＝「（天気・見通しが）暗い、悪い」。Despite と「幸い雨は最後まで降らなかった」から、予報は悪かったと分かる。lavish（豪華な）、fragile（壊れやすい）、vacant（空いている）は予報に合わない。

questions.q: The professor's lecture was so ____ that many students struggled to follow it. She kept jumping from topic to topic without explaining how they were connected.
choices: concise
punctual
incoherent
unanimous
questions.why: incoherent＝「まとまりのない、筋の通らない」。話題が飛び、つながりを説明しない、が根拠。concise（簡潔な）は逆の意味。punctual（時間を守る）、unanimous（満場一致の）は講義の説明にならない。

questions.q: After months of difficult negotiations, the two companies finally reached a ____, with each side agreeing to give up some of its original demands.
choices: deficit
monopoly
compromise
surplus
questions.why: reach a compromise＝「妥協に至る」。お互いに要求の一部をあきらめた、が妥協の中身。deficit（赤字）、monopoly（独占）、surplus（黒字・余剰）は交渉の結果として合わない。

questions.q: The hikers were forced to ____ their attempt to reach the summit when a thick fog rolled in and made the narrow path too dangerous to follow.
choices: enforce
abort
simulate
inherit
questions.why: abort＝「（途中で）中止する」。霧で道が危険になり、登頂の試みをやめた。enforce（施行する）、simulate（模擬実験する）、inherit（受け継ぐ）は were forced to と合わない。

questions.q: Jenna is extremely ____ about her work. She checks every report three times before submitting it, so her manager almost never finds any mistakes.
choices: reluctant
hostile
meticulous
indifferent
questions.why: meticulous＝「細心の、きちょうめんな」。3回確認する・ミスがほぼ無い、が具体例。indifferent（無関心な）は逆。reluctant（気が進まない）、hostile（敵意のある）も例と合わない。

questions.q: The new medicine can ____ the symptoms of the illness, but it cannot actually cure it, so patients still need to have regular checkups.
choices: alleviate
dictate
confiscate
fabricate
questions.why: alleviate＝「（苦痛・症状を）和らげる」。but で「治すことはできない」と続くので、症状を軽くする意味が入る。dictate（命じる）、confiscate（没収する）、fabricate（でっち上げる）は症状に使わない。

questions.q: Many residents were ____ of the developer's promises, as the same company had failed to complete a similar project in the neighboring town.
choices: fond
ashamed
envious
skeptical
questions.why: be skeptical of ～＝「～を疑っている」。隣町で同じ会社が計画を終えられなかった、が疑う理由。fond of（好きだ）、ashamed of（恥じる）、envious of（うらやむ）は理由とつながらない。

questions.q:
A: I can't believe how much the price of coffee has gone up this year.
B: I know. Experts say it's because of a ____ of beans caused by poor harvests in several countries.
choices: scarcity
fraction
venue
hazard
questions.why: scarcity＝「不足、欠乏」。不作で豆が足りず値上がりした、という因果。fraction（一部分）、venue（会場）、hazard（危険）では値上がりの理由にならない。

questions.q: The author's latest novel received ____ praise from critics, who all agreed that it was the finest book she had ever written.
choices: tentative
obsolete
sluggish
unanimous
questions.why: unanimous＝「満場一致の」。批評家が全員（all agreed）最高傑作と認めた。tentative（仮の・ためらいがちな）は all agreed と合わない。obsolete（時代遅れの）、sluggish（のろい）も不可。

questions.q: The city council plans to ____ the old textile factory into a community center with a library, a gym, and studios for local artists.
choices: deprive
exempt
dissuade
convert
questions.why: convert A into B＝「AをBに改造する」。into と組むのは convert。deprive A of B（奪う）、exempt A from B（免除する）、dissuade A from ～ing（思いとどまらせる）は前置詞も意味も合わない。

questions.q: The small family bakery has managed to ____ despite strong competition from supermarket chains, mainly because customers love its traditional recipes.
choices: thrive
dwindle
falter
recede
questions.why: thrive＝「繁盛する」。despite（競争にもかかわらず）と「客に愛されている」から、うまくいっている意味。dwindle（だんだん減る）、falter（ぐらつく）、recede（後退する）は逆の流れ。

questions.q: Because the assembly instructions were so ____, many customers put the bookshelf together incorrectly and had to call the company for help.
choices: ambiguous
generous
authentic
vigorous
questions.why: ambiguous＝「あいまいな、2通りに取れる」。説明書のせいで組み立てを間違えた、という結果から。generous（気前のよい）、authentic（本物の）、vigorous（活発な）は説明書の欠点にならない。

questions.q: The athlete's ____ to recover from a serious knee injury and win a gold medal two years later inspired many young people across the country.
choices: hesitation
imitation
consumption
determination
questions.why: determination to do＝「～しようという固い決意」。大けがから立ち直り金メダル、が人々を励ました。hesitation（ためらい）は逆。imitation（模倣）、consumption（消費）は意味が通らない。

questions.q: Tom tried to ____ his disappointment when he was not chosen for the promotion, but his colleagues could tell from his face that he was upset.
choices: conceal
nominate
assemble
cultivate
questions.why: conceal＝「隠す」。but で「顔を見れば分かった」と続くので、隠そうとした。nominate（指名する）、assemble（組み立てる）、cultivate（耕す・育てる）は失望に使わない。

questions.q: Online reviews can have a ____ effect on small restaurants. Just a few negative comments may be enough to drive customers away for months.
choices: nominal
cordial
profound
redundant
questions.why: profound effect＝「大きな影響」。数件の悪い口コミで何か月も客が離れる、が影響の大きさ。nominal（名ばかりの・わずかな）は逆。cordial（心からの）、redundant（余分な）も合わない。

questions.q: Visitors are not allowed to touch the artworks in the museum, as even small amounts of oil from human skin can ____ the surface of old paintings.
choices: reinforce
degrade
illuminate
replicate
questions.why: degrade＝「劣化させる」。触ってはいけない理由なので、悪い影響を表す語。reinforce（補強する）、illuminate（照らす）、replicate（複製する）は禁止の理由にならない。

questions.q: After the merger, several senior managers ____ from the company because they strongly disagreed with the new owner's plans for the business.
choices: inquired
resigned
collided
emerged
questions.why: resign from ～＝「～を辞職する」。新しい経営者の方針に反対だった、が理由。inquired（尋ねた）、collided（衝突した）、emerged（現れた）は from the company と組んでも意味を成さない。

questions.q: Scientists warn that if fish populations continue to ____ at the current rate, many coastal communities could lose their main source of income.
choices: flourish
linger
dwindle
prevail
questions.why: dwindle＝「だんだん減る」。魚が減れば漁村が収入を失う、という警告。flourish（栄える）では収入を失う理由にならない。linger（長引く）、prevail（広まる）も不可。

questions.q: The manager praised Kenji for his ____ response to the customer's complaint. He apologized immediately and offered a full refund within minutes.
choices: vague
dormant
prompt
brittle
questions.why: prompt＝「迅速な」。すぐ謝り数分で返金、が根拠。vague（あいまいな）、dormant（休止中の）、brittle（もろい）では褒める理由にならない。

questions.q: Although the twin sisters look almost ____, people who know them well can easily tell them apart by their voices and the way they laugh.
choices: incompatible
insistent
indispensable
indistinguishable
questions.why: indistinguishable＝「区別がつかない」。Although と tell them apart（見分ける）から、見た目はそっくりだと分かる。incompatible（相性が悪い）、insistent（しつこい）、indispensable（不可欠な）は形が似ているだけ。

questions.q: The documentary gives a ____ account of daily life in a remote mountain village, clearly showing both the joys and the hardships of the residents.
choices: frantic
reckless
vivid
stale
questions.why: vivid account＝「生き生きとした描写」。喜びも苦労もはっきり見せる、が根拠。frantic（取り乱した）、reckless（無謀な）、stale（新鮮でない）は良い描写の意味にならない。

questions.q: Visitors to the national park are reminded that feeding the wild animals is strictly ____ and can result in a heavy fine.
choices: inevitable
contagious
prohibited
negligible
questions.why: prohibited＝「禁止されている」。重い罰金になる、が根拠。inevitable（避けられない）、contagious（伝染性の）、negligible（ごくわずかな）は罰金と結びつかない。

questions.q: The new employee felt ____ at her first team meeting because she did not know anyone and was unsure whether she was allowed to speak.
choices: apprehensive
jubilant
lenient
spacious
questions.why: apprehensive＝「不安な、心配な」。知り合いがおらず発言してよいか分からない、が理由。jubilant（大喜びの）は逆。lenient（寛大な）、spacious（広々とした）は気持ちを表さない。

questions.q: Recent discoveries have ____ the long-held belief that dinosaurs were slow, cold-blooded creatures, showing that many of them were actually active and fast.
choices: endured
refuted
nurtured
embraced
questions.why: refute＝「（説を）誤りだと証明する」。実は活発で速かったと示した、が根拠。embraced（受け入れた）は逆。endured（耐えた）、nurtured（育てた）は説に使わない。

questions.q: The charity relies almost entirely on ____ from local businesses and individuals to fund the free meals it provides for elderly residents.
choices: allegations
contributions
restrictions
quarrels
questions.why: contribution＝「寄付」。無料の食事の資金を何に頼るか、なので寄付。allegations（申し立て）、restrictions（制限）、quarrels（口論）は資金にならない。

questions.q: The report criticized the company for its ____ use of plastic packaging, pointing out that most of it was unnecessary and could easily be replaced with paper.
choices: frugal
excessive
sparse
sincere
questions.why: excessive＝「過剰な」。ほとんどが不要だった、が批判の中身。frugal（倹約的な）、sparse（まばらな）は逆。sincere（誠実な）は批判と合わない。

questions.q:
A: Did you hear that the café on Pine Street is closing?
B: Yes. The owner said rising rent means the business is no longer financially ____, so she's moving to a cheaper area.
choices: viable
fluent
sedentary
impartial
questions.why: financially viable＝「経営的に成り立つ」。家賃が上がり続けられないので安い地域へ移る。fluent（流ちょうな）、sedentary（座りがちな）、impartial（公平な）は事業の状態を表さない。

questions.q: Many parents worry that children who spend several hours a day looking at screens may be more ____ to eye problems and poor sleep.
choices: obedient
adjacent
indebted
susceptible
questions.why: be susceptible to ～＝「～にかかりやすい」。画面を長く見る子は目の問題や睡眠不足になりやすい。obedient to（従順な）、adjacent to（隣接した）、indebted to（恩がある）は病気に使わない。

questions.q: The hotel staff went out of their way to ____ the guests' special requests, such as preparing a vegetarian breakfast and arranging an early check-in.
choices: contaminate
intimidate
deteriorate
accommodate
questions.why: accommodate a request＝「要望に応える」。菜食の朝食・早いチェックインの手配が具体例。contaminate（汚染する）、intimidate（おどす）、deteriorate（悪化する）は合わない。

questions.q: The company had to ____ its plans to open a new branch overseas after sales fell sharply in the first half of the year.
choices: hand down
scale back
phase in
fill out
questions.why: scale back＝「（計画を）縮小する」。売上の急落が理由。hand down（伝える）、phase in（段階的に導入する）、fill out（記入する）は売上が落ちた時の対応として合わない。

questions.q: When Martin lost his job last spring, several of his close friends ____ to help him pay his rent until he found new work.
choices: chipped in
stood out
pulled through
ran over
questions.why: chip in＝「（お金を）出し合う」。家賃を払う手助け、なのでお金を出し合った。stood out（目立った）、pulled through（切り抜けた）、ran over（ひいた・あふれた）は合わない。

questions.q: The talks between the two firms nearly ____ when neither side would accept the other's terms, but a last-minute offer saved the deal.
choices: took after
broke down
wore off
looked up
questions.why: break down＝「（交渉が）決裂する」。どちらも条件をのまず、最後の提案で救われた。took after（似ている）、wore off（薄れた）、looked up（良くなった）は交渉の危機を表さない。

questions.q: Lisa's idea of opening a bookstore with a café seemed risky at first, but it ____ well, and she now runs three shops in the city.
choices: backed down
dropped by
panned out
cut in
questions.why: pan out＝「（計画が）うまくいく」。今では3店舗、が結果。backed down（引き下がった）、dropped by（立ち寄った）、cut in（割り込んだ）は計画の結果を表さない。

questions.q: Sarah ____ a bad cold the day before her big presentation, so her colleague had to give it in her place.
choices: came up with
got away with
put up with
came down with
questions.why: come down with ～＝「（病気に）かかる」。同僚が代わりに発表した理由。came up with（思いついた）、got away with（うまく逃れた）、put up with（我慢した）は風邪と組まない。

questions.q: Even when the whole team argued that the deadline was unrealistic, the manager refused to ____ and insisted that the project be finished on time.
choices: lay off
back down
sum up
pass out
questions.why: back down＝「（主張を）引っ込める、折れる」。refused to と「期限通りにと言い張った」から、譲らなかった。lay off（解雇する）、sum up（要約する）、pass out（気を失う）は合わない。

questions.q: Researchers are still trying to ____ the exact reason why some seabirds return to the same nest year after year.
choices: pin down
wear out
run up
strike up
questions.why: pin down＝「（原因などを）突き止める」。理由をはっきりさせようとしている。wear out（すり減らす）、run up（（借金を）ためる）、strike up（（会話を）始める）は reason と組まない。

questions.q: The heavy snow ____ the delivery trucks for two days, so many stores in the area ran out of fresh vegetables.
choices: gave off
made up
turned in
held up
questions.why: hold up＝「遅らせる、足止めする」。トラックが来ず野菜が売り切れた。gave off（（においを）出した）、made up（作り上げた）、turned in（提出した）は合わない。

questions.q: After years of working long hours, Diana decided to ____ on her responsibilities at work so that she could spend more time with her children.
choices: cut back
cash in
look on
frown on
questions.why: cut back on ～＝「～を減らす」。子どもとの時間を増やすため仕事を減らす。cash in on（～につけ込む）、look on（傍観する）、frown on（～に眉をひそめる）は目的と合わない。

questions.q: The new puzzle app ____ quickly among teenagers, and within a month it had been downloaded more than a million times.
choices: fell apart
gave out
caught on
saw off
questions.why: catch on＝「流行する、人気が出る」。1か月で100万回以上ダウンロード、が根拠。fell apart（ばらばらになった）、gave out（尽きた）、saw off（見送った）は人気を表さない。

questions.q: The two neighbors had a long-running ____ over the tall fence between their gardens, which finally ended when they agreed to share the cost of a lower one.
choices: remedy
dispute
pledge
tribute
questions.why: dispute＝「争い、口論」。フェンスをめぐる長い対立が、費用を分け合うことで終わった。remedy（治療法）、pledge（誓約）、tribute（賛辞）は終わる対立にならない。

questions.q: Even the speaker's friendly jokes failed to ____ the tension in the room, and the audience remained silent and uneasy for the rest of his talk.
choices: extract
harness
commemorate
defuse
questions.why: defuse the tension＝「緊張を和らげる」。冗談でも和らがず、聞き手は落ち着かないまま。extract（抜き出す）、harness（利用する）、commemorate（記念する）は tension と合わない。

questions.q: Opening a second restaurant downtown proved highly ____ for the chef, and within a year it was earning twice as much as her original location.
choices: lucrative
hollow
timid
feeble
questions.why: lucrative＝「もうかる」。1年で元の店の2倍を稼いだ、が根拠。hollow（中身のない）、timid（臆病な）、feeble（弱々しい）は利益の話に合わない。

questions.q: After forty years as the head of the family business, Mr. Grant finally agreed to ____ control to his daughter and retire to the countryside.
choices: verify
oppress
relinquish
assert
questions.why: relinquish control to ～＝「～に支配権を譲る」。引退するので娘に経営を渡す。assert（主張する）は逆の向きで、to his daughter とも組まない。verify（確かめる）、oppress（抑圧する）も合わない。

questions.q: Many workers find data entry ____ because it involves typing the same kinds of numbers into a computer for hours without any variety.
choices: eloquent
tedious
versatile
hearty
questions.why: tedious＝「退屈な、うんざりする」。同じ数字を何時間も変化なく打ち込む、が理由。eloquent（雄弁な）、versatile（多才な）、hearty（心のこもった）は合わない。

questions.q: The company will ____ employees for any travel expenses, such as train tickets and hotel bills, as long as they submit the original receipts within a month.
choices: console
exploit
interrogate
reimburse
questions.why: reimburse A for B＝「AにBを払い戻す」。領収書を出せば交通費・宿泊費を返す。console（慰める）、exploit（搾取する）、interrogate（尋問する）は経費の話にならない。

questions.q: The city has taken ____ measures to reduce traffic in the downtown area, including banning private cars from several main streets on weekends.
choices: trivial
tender
drastic
fertile
questions.why: drastic measures＝「思い切った対策」。週末に大通りから自家用車を締め出す、が具体例。trivial（ささいな）は具体例と逆。tender（優しい）、fertile（肥えた）は合わない。

questions.q: It took the researcher nearly two years to ____ a complete list of the plant species growing on the remote island.
choices: compile
dismiss
oblige
erode
questions.why: compile a list＝「一覧をまとめる」。2年かけて島の植物の完全な一覧を作った。dismiss（退ける）、oblige（義務を負わせる）、erode（浸食する）は a list と合わない。

questions.q: Kate ____ deleted an important file while cleaning up her computer, so she had to ask a technician to help her recover it.
choices: generously
gracefully
fiercely
inadvertently
questions.why: inadvertently＝「うっかり、不注意で」。整理中に大事なファイルを消してしまい、復元を頼んだ。generously（気前よく）、gracefully（優雅に）、fiercely（激しく）は合わない。

questions.q: Because several committee members were sick, the chairperson decided to ____ the meeting until the following week.
choices: exclaim
deduct
adjourn
venture
questions.why: adjourn＝「（会議を）延期する、休会にする」。委員が病気なので翌週に延ばした。exclaim（叫ぶ）、deduct（差し引く）、venture（思い切ってする）は the meeting until … と組まない。

questions.q:
A: Are you still thinking of buying that old house by the lake?
B: No. The inspector found that its foundation was ____, so repairing it would cost more than the house itself.
choices: eligible
defective
thrifty
nimble
questions.why: defective＝「欠陥のある」。修理費が家より高くなるので買わない。eligible（資格のある）、thrifty（倹約的な）、nimble（すばしこい）は土台の説明にならない。

questions.q: Dark clouds gathered over the bay, and the fishermen hurried back to the harbor after hearing the ____ sound of thunder in the distance.
choices: ominous
soothing
festive
humble
questions.why: ominous＝「不吉な、嫌な予感がする」。雷の音を聞いて急いで港へ戻った。soothing（心を落ち着かせる）、festive（お祭りの）では急いで戻る理由にならない。

questions.q: The store saw a sudden ____ in demand for umbrellas when the weather service predicted a week of heavy rain.
choices: lapse
slump
haven
surge
questions.why: surge in demand＝「需要の急増」。大雨の予報で傘が急に売れた。slump（不振）は逆。lapse（ちょっとした誤り）、haven（避難所）は合わない。

questions.q: Health officials hope the new vaccine will help ____ the disease entirely, so that no new cases appear anywhere in the region.
choices: proclaim
eradicate
mimic
flatter
questions.why: eradicate＝「根絶する」。新しい患者がどこにも出ないように、病気を完全になくす。proclaim（宣言する）、mimic（まねる）、flatter（お世辞を言う）は合わない。

questions.q: The ____ reporter called the office every day for three weeks until the manager finally agreed to an interview.
choices: bashful
idle
tenacious
mundane
questions.why: tenacious＝「粘り強い」。3週間毎日電話して取材にこぎつけた。bashful（恥ずかしがりの）、idle（怠けた）は行動と逆。mundane（ありふれた）は人の性質に合わない。

questions.q: The student's excuse for missing the exam sounded ____ at first, but the teacher later found out that he had actually gone to a concert that day.
choices: plausible
absurd
furious
opaque
questions.why: plausible＝「もっともらしい」。but の後で「実はコンサートに行っていた」と分かったので、最初は本当らしく聞こえた。absurd（ばかげた）では but の逆接にならない。

questions.q: The airline was forced to ____ the number of flights to the island during the winter months because so few passengers were traveling there.
choices: curtail
escalate
ratify
commend
questions.why: curtail＝「削減する、切り詰める」。乗客が少ないので便を減らした。escalate（拡大させる）は逆。ratify（批准する）、commend（ほめる）は合わない。

questions.q: Although the old ship had been lying at the bottom of the lake for over a century, divers were surprised to find that most of it was still ____.
choices: adrift
intact
sober
eager
questions.why: intact＝「無傷の、元のままの」。100年以上沈んでいたのに、ほとんど壊れていなかったので驚いた。adrift（漂流して）は湖の底の船に合わない。sober（しらふの）、eager（熱心な）も合わない。

questions.q:
A: Why did Ryan quit the soccer team?
B: He said the coach's constant criticism had become ____, and he just didn't enjoy playing anymore.
choices: invaluable
imminent
edible
unbearable
questions.why: unbearable＝「耐えられない」。絶え間ない批判に耐えられず、楽しめなくなってやめた。invaluable（非常に貴重な）は逆。imminent（差し迫った）、edible（食べられる）は合わない。

questions.q: Before signing the contract, Ms. Hale asked her lawyer to ____ every clause carefully to make sure there were no hidden fees.
choices: overlook
stimulate
scrutinize
auction
questions.why: scrutinize＝「綿密に調べる」。隠れた費用が無いか、条項を一つ一つ注意して見る。overlook（見落とす）は carefully と逆。stimulate（刺激する）、auction（競売にかける）は合わない。

questions.q: When the Johnsons helped their new neighbors move in, the neighbors ____ by inviting them over for a home-cooked dinner the following weekend.
choices: dissolved
retaliated
perished
reciprocated
questions.why: reciprocate＝「（好意に）お返しをする」。引っ越しを手伝ってもらい、夕食に招いてお返しした。retaliate（仕返しする）は悪いことへの仕返しで合わない。

questions.q: The ____ old theater, with its broken windows and leaking roof, was finally restored after a local group raised enough money to repair it.
choices: immaculate
prosperous
dilapidated
nocturnal
questions.why: dilapidated＝「荒れ果てた、老朽化した」。窓が割れ屋根が雨漏りしている、が根拠。immaculate（しみ一つない）は逆。prosperous（繁栄した）、nocturnal（夜行性の）は合わない。

questions.q: Because each presenter had only three minutes, the organizers asked them to keep their explanations ____ and to focus on just one main point.
choices: succinct
elaborate
perpetual
rigid
questions.why: succinct＝「簡潔な」。持ち時間3分なので短く、要点1つに。elaborate（手の込んだ）は逆。perpetual（永遠の）、rigid（堅い）は合わない。

questions.q: The farmer put up a tall fence around the field to ____ deer from eating the young vegetable plants.
choices: lure
deter
nourish
uphold
questions.why: deter A from doing＝「Aに～するのを思いとどまらせる」。高い柵でシカに野菜を食べさせない。lure（おびき寄せる）は逆。nourish（栄養を与える）、uphold（支持する）は合わない。

questions.q: Fresh fish is ____ in the small coastal town, so restaurants there can offer seafood dishes at much lower prices than those in the city.
choices: absent
stern
abundant
obscure
questions.why: abundant＝「豊富な」。魚がたくさんあるので安く出せる。absent（無い）では安くできる理由にならない。stern（厳格な）、obscure（あいまいな）は合わない。

questions.q: Students who ____ until the night before an exam often find that they do not have enough time to review all the material.
choices: collaborate
procrastinate
recite
migrate
questions.why: procrastinate＝「先延ばしにする」。前の晩まで勉強を先延ばしすると、復習の時間が足りない。collaborate（協力する）、recite（暗唱する）、migrate（移住する）は合わない。

questions.q: The factory follows ____ safety rules, and any worker who enters the production area without a helmet is immediately sent home.
choices: lax
cozy
savage
stringent
questions.why: stringent＝「厳しい」。ヘルメットが無いとすぐ帰宅させられる、が具体例。lax（緩い）は逆。cozy（居心地のよい）、savage（どう猛な）は合わない。

questions.q:
A: How was your trip to the mountains?
B: Wonderful. The view from the top was so ____ that I forgot how tired I was from the long climb.
choices: breathtaking
monotonous
dreary
stagnant
questions.why: breathtaking＝「息をのむほど美しい」。Wonderful と、疲れを忘れたほど、が根拠。monotonous（単調な）、dreary（わびしい）、stagnant（よどんだ）は良い意味にならない。

questions.q: Poor lighting in the old library can ____ students' ability to read for long periods, so the school plans to install new lamps this summer.
choices: hinder
enhance
salute
glorify
questions.why: hinder＝「妨げる」。暗い照明が長く読む妨げになるので新しい照明を付ける。enhance（高める）では照明を替える理由にならない。salute（敬礼する）、glorify（たたえる）は合わない。

questions.q: Attendance at the safety training is ____ for all new staff, and anyone who misses it will not be allowed to start work until they complete it.
choices: optional
luxurious
obligatory
cautious
questions.why: obligatory＝「義務の、必須の」。受けないと仕事を始められない、が根拠。optional（任意の）は逆。luxurious（ぜいたくな）、cautious（用心深い）は合わない。

questions.q: The outdoor concert was ____ at the last minute because the lead singer had lost her voice, and fans were promised full refunds.
choices: brought about
called off
set out
turned up
questions.why: call off＝「中止する」。歌手の声が出ず、全額返金。brought about（引き起こした）、set out（出発した）、turned up（現れた）は合わない。

questions.q: It took Owen several months to ____ the shock of losing his job, but he eventually found a new position that he enjoyed even more.
choices: give in
run into
take over
get over
questions.why: get over＝「（ショック・病気から）立ち直る」。数か月かかったが、もっと好きな仕事が見つかった。give in（屈する）、run into（偶然会う）、take over（引き継ぐ）は the shock と合わない。

questions.q: The engineers are still ____ what caused the bridge's lights to stop working last night, and they expect to have an answer by Friday.
choices: looking into
taking in
setting up
holding back
questions.why: look into＝「調べる」。原因を調べていて、金曜までに答えが出る見込み。taking in（取り入れる・だます）、setting up（設置する）、holding back（抑える）は what caused … と合わない。

questions.q: Marcus keeps ____ going to the dentist because he is afraid it will hurt, but his toothache is getting worse every day.
choices: showing off
putting off
giving away
filling in
questions.why: put off doing＝「～するのを先延ばしにする」。痛いのが怖くて歯医者に行かず、歯痛がひどくなる。showing off（見せびらかす）、giving away（手放す）、filling in（記入する）は合わない。

questions.q: Several new problems ____ during the test run of the software, so the launch was delayed by another two weeks.
choices: wiped out
handed in
cropped up
laid down
questions.why: crop up＝「（問題が）不意に起こる」。試運転で問題が出て発売が延びた。wiped out（全滅させた）、handed in（提出した）、laid down（定めた）は主語の problems と合わない。

questions.q: The manager asked her team to ____ a detailed plan for the product launch by the end of the week.
choices: break in
hang up
pour in
draw up
questions.why: draw up a plan＝「計画を作成する」。週末までに詳しい計画を作る。break in（押し入る・慣らす）、hang up（電話を切る）、pour in（殺到する）は a plan と合わない。

questions.q: After the long hike, Ben was so tired that he ____ on the sofa as soon as he got home and slept until the next morning.
choices: stepped up
dozed off
signed up
sorted out
questions.why: doze off＝「うとうと眠り込む」。疲れてソファで寝てしまい、朝まで寝た。stepped up（強化した）、signed up（申し込んだ）、sorted out（解決した）は合わない。

questions.q: Doctors have not ____ the possibility that the patient's headaches are caused by stress, so they have suggested some relaxation exercises.
choices: handed out
brushed up
torn off
ruled out
questions.why: rule out＝「（可能性を）除外する」。ストレスが原因の可能性を消していないので、リラックスの運動を勧めた。handed out（配った）、brushed up（磨き直した）、torn off（引きちぎった）は the possibility と合わない。

questions.q: Sales of the new phone were slow at first, but they began to ____ after a popular video blogger praised it.
choices: let down
tear down
pick up
hand over
questions.why: pick up＝「（売上・景気が）持ち直す」。but で「最初は不調」と逆になる。let down（がっかりさせる）、tear down（取り壊す）、hand over（手渡す）は売上の動きにならない。

questions.q: The two friends ____ after a disagreement about money, and they did not speak to each other for nearly a year.
choices: fell out
showed up
kept on
got along
questions.why: fall out＝「仲たがいする」。お金のことでもめて1年近く口をきかなかった。got along（仲よくした）は逆。showed up（現れた）、kept on（続けた）は合わない。

parts.title: 大問2 長文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 約250語の説明文（3段落）の空所3つに入る語句を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: 空所の前後1文ずつが根拠。In other words / As a result の後ろは前の内容のまとめ・結果になる。つなぎ語の空所は、前後が「逆接・追加・具体例・裏づけ」のどれかを先に決めてから選ぶ。
parts.intro: Read each passage and choose the best word or phrase from the four choices for each numbered blank.

sets.passage:
The Return of the Night Sky

For most of human history, people could look up on a clear night and see thousands of stars. Today, however, artificial lighting from streets, buildings, and advertisements has made the night sky far brighter than it would naturally be. In many large cities, residents can see fewer than twenty stars. This so-called light pollution is not just a problem for amateur astronomers. Studies suggest that it can disturb the sleep of people living nearby and confuse animals that rely on darkness, such as moths and migrating birds. In other words, excessive light ( 1 ).

In response, a number of towns have begun taking steps to reduce unnecessary lighting. The small town of Elmsworth, for example, replaced its streetlights with lamps that point downward and automatically dim after midnight. Officials were initially concerned that residents would feel unsafe walking home at night. ( 2 ), surveys conducted a year later found that most people had hardly noticed the change, and the town's electricity bill fell by nearly 40 percent.

Elmsworth's success has also brought unexpected benefits. Because its sky is now dark enough to see the Milky Way, the town has started attracting visitors who want to experience stargazing. Local hotels offer guided night-sky tours, and a nearby farm has opened a small observatory. Some experts believe that other communities could ( 3 ). If they are right, protecting darkness may turn out to be good not only for nature but also for business.

choices: affects far more than our view of the stars
is mainly a problem in rural areas
helps animals find food more easily
has become less common in recent years
questions.why: 直前で、睡眠の妨げや動物の混乱など、星が見えないこと以外の害が挙がっている。In other words でまとめるので「星の眺め以外にも影響する」。田舎の問題・動物を助ける・減っている、は本文と逆か無関係。

choices: For this reason
Similarly
In addition
As it turned out
questions.why: 前の文は「住民が不安になると心配した」、後ろは「ほとんど気づかなかった」。心配が外れた結果なので「結局のところ」。For this reason（このため）、Similarly（同様に）、In addition（さらに）は前後の食い違いを表せない。

choices: ignore the needs of local businesses
install brighter lights to attract tourists
turn their dark skies into a source of income
stop visitors from entering at night
questions.why: 前の文で星空ツアーや観測所が観光客を呼んでいる。最後の文の good for business につながるのは「暗い空を収入源にする」。明るい照明を増やす、は本文の主張と逆。

sets.passage:
Lessons from Ant Traffic

Anyone who has watched a line of ants carrying food back to their nest may have noticed something surprising: ants rarely seem to get stuck in traffic jams. Even when thousands of them use the same narrow trail, the flow continues smoothly. Human drivers, by contrast, often find themselves stopped on busy roads. This difference has led some scientists to study ants in the hope that they ( 1 ).

One reason ants avoid jams appears to be that they do not compete with one another. A driver may try to overtake other cars or change lanes to save a few seconds, which often forces those behind to brake suddenly. Ants, on the other hand, keep a steady pace and do not try to pass those in front of them. Researchers also found that when a trail becomes extremely crowded, ants ( 2 ). Rather than pushing forward, some simply wait at the nest until the trail clears, which prevents the situation from getting worse.

Engineers believe these findings could become useful as self-driving cars grow more common. Unlike human drivers, such vehicles could be programmed to share information and adjust their speed together, much like a colony of ants. ( 3 ), computer simulations based on ant behavior have shown that traffic could move up to 20 percent faster if all cars followed similar rules. Of course, human roads are far more complicated than ant trails, but nature may still offer valuable ideas for solving everyday problems.

choices: could be trained to carry heavier objects
would stop building nests near roads
might reveal ways to improve the movement of vehicles
may explain why drivers prefer large cars
questions.why: 直前で「アリは渋滞しないが人間の車はする」と比べている。研究の目的は車の流れを良くするヒントを得ること。重い物を運ぶ・巣の場所・大きな車の好みは渋滞と関係ない。

choices: reduce the number of individuals that set out
begin to move much more quickly
leave the trail to search for new food
start to compete for the best positions
questions.why: 続く文で「前に進まず巣で待つアリもいる」とある。つまり出発する数を減らす。速く動く・競う、は第2段落の内容と逆。

choices: Indeed
Nevertheless
Otherwise
Even so
questions.why: 前の文「車が協調できれば」を、後ろの文が「シミュレーションで最大20%速くなった」と裏づけている。だから「実際に」。Nevertheless / Even so（それでも）は逆接、Otherwise（さもなければ）は条件で、どれも合わない。

sets.passage:
Paying with Time

In most economies, people exchange goods and services for money. In recent decades, however, a different system known as "time banking" has spread to communities around the world. In a time bank, members earn credits by helping others, and one hour of work always earns one credit, no matter what the task is. A retired teacher who spends an hour tutoring a child earns exactly the same as someone who spends an hour repairing a fence. Members can then use their credits to receive help from others. Supporters say this system ( 1 ).

Time banks have proved particularly valuable for people who have skills but little money. At the Harlow Valley Time Bank, for example, many members are elderly residents who live alone. Some of them used to feel that they had nothing left to offer society. Through the time bank, however, they have found ways to share their knowledge, such as teaching cooking or knitting. As a result, many say that they ( 2 ). Organizers also report that members are more likely to know and trust their neighbors.

Despite these benefits, time banks face certain difficulties. Because no money is involved, they often depend on a single volunteer coordinator who matches members with tasks, and when that person leaves, the whole system can quickly fall apart. ( 3 ), some members are reluctant to ask for help, even when they have plenty of credits to spend. To overcome these challenges, some time banks now use simple smartphone apps that let members find each other directly.

choices: rewards those with professional qualifications
treats everyone's time as equally valuable
allows members to exchange credits for cash
was designed mainly for large businesses
questions.why: どんな仕事でも1時間＝1クレジットで、元教師も柵の修理も同じ。つまり全員の時間を同じ価値として扱う。資格のある人を優遇・現金に替える、は本文と逆。

choices: prefer to spend time on their own
have decided to move to the city
feel more connected to their community
earn more money than before
questions.why: 一人暮らしの高齢者が知識を分け合うようになった結果。次の文の「近所の人を知り信頼する」とも合う。一人で過ごしたい・都会へ引っ越す・収入が増える、は本文に無い（お金は使わない仕組み）。

choices: As a result
In addition
In contrast
For this reason
questions.why: 「調整役が辞めると崩れる」に続けて「助けを頼みたがらない人がいる」と、2つ目の問題を足している。だから「さらに」。As a result / For this reason は因果だが、調整役の話と頼みにくさは因果ではない。In contrast（対照的に）も合わない。

sets.passage:
Rediscovering Old Apples

A century ago, farmers in some regions grew hundreds of different varieties of apples. Each had its own flavor, color, and season, and many were suited to particular uses, such as baking, making juice, or storing through the winter. Today, however, most supermarkets sell only a handful of varieties. These were chosen mainly because they look attractive, travel well, and stay fresh for a long time on store shelves. As a result, many traditional varieties ( 1 ).

In recent years, a growing number of enthusiasts have set out to find and save these forgotten apples. Members of one group, the Ridgefield Orchard Society, search old farms and abandoned gardens for trees that may be the last of their kind. When they find one, they cut small branches from it and attach them to young trees, a technique that allows the variety to be reproduced exactly. The work is slow, however, because ( 2 ). Members often have to compare the fruit with descriptions and drawings in old books before they can be confident about what they have found.

Supporters argue that protecting rare varieties is more than just a hobby. Some old apples are naturally resistant to certain diseases, which could make them useful to scientists developing new varieties that require fewer chemicals. ( 3 ), many chefs and cider makers have become interested in their unusual flavors. The society now sells young trees to the public, hoping that more people will plant them in their own gardens.

choices: are now sold mainly overseas
have been grown in greater numbers
are used only for making juice
have almost disappeared
questions.why: スーパーは見た目・輸送・日持ちで選んだ数種類しか売らない。As a result なので、昔の品種は消えかけている。次の段落の「忘れられたリンゴを救う」ともつながる。たくさん育てられている、は逆。

choices: most farmers refuse to let them visit
identifying a tree's variety can be extremely difficult
young trees need very little care
the branches are too heavy to carry
questions.why: 続く文で「古い本の記述や絵と比べないと確信できない」とある。品種を見分けるのが難しいから時間がかかる。農家が断る・枝が重い、は本文に無い。

choices: Instead
Otherwise
Even so
Moreover
questions.why: 前の文は「病気に強く科学者に役立つ」、後ろは「シェフやサイダー職人も味に関心」。守る理由を2つ並べているので「さらに」。Instead（代わりに）、Otherwise（さもなければ）、Even so（それでも）は合わない。

sets.passage:
Fixing Things Together

In many towns, broken household items such as toasters, lamps, and bicycles are simply thrown away, often because repairing them seems more expensive than buying new ones. A growing number of volunteers, however, are trying to change this habit by running events known as repair cafés. At these monthly gatherings, residents bring in damaged goods, and skilled volunteers show them how to fix the items themselves, free of charge. Common repairs include replacing a broken switch or sewing up a torn jacket. Organizers say their goal is not only to reduce waste but also to ( 1 ).

One reason repair cafés are needed is that many modern products are difficult to open. Some are glued shut, and others can only be opened with special tools that ordinary people do not own. Manufacturers argue that such designs make products thinner, lighter, and safer. ( 2 ), critics point out that they also make it much harder for consumers to replace a single worn-out part, forcing them to buy a whole new device instead.

The cafés have also had effects that go beyond repairs. Volunteers report that many visitors stay long after their items are fixed, chatting over coffee with neighbors they had never met before. Others have formed lasting friendships. In one town, a retired electrician who started volunteering at a café said that teaching others gave him a new sense of purpose after he stopped working. For many participants, then, repair cafés have become ( 3 ).

choices: persuade manufacturers to lower their prices
train volunteers to become professional repairers
sell secondhand goods to local residents
help people gain confidence in fixing things on their own
questions.why: 直前で、ボランティアが「自分で直す方法を教える」とある。ごみを減らすだけでなく、自分で直せる自信を持たせるのが目的。値下げ・プロの育成・中古品の販売は本文に無い。

choices: As a result
On the other hand
For instance
In the same way
questions.why: 前はメーカーの言い分（薄く安全になる）、後ろは批判する側の言い分（部品を替えられない）。立場が反対なので「一方で」。As a result（その結果）、For instance（例えば）、In the same way（同様に）はつながらない。

choices: a valuable way of building connections within the community
a place where only experts are welcome
a cause of conflict between neighbors
a business that earns large profits
questions.why: 修理の後も近所の人と話し込む、元電気技師が生きがいを得た、が直前の例。修理を超えて「地域のつながりを作る場」になった。専門家だけ・対立・大きな利益は本文と合わない。

sets.passage:
Pens or Keyboards?

Although most university students now take notes on laptops, some researchers believe that writing by hand may be better for learning. In one study, two groups of students watched the same lecture. One group typed their notes, while the other wrote them with pens. Both groups were allowed to review their notes before the test. When they were tested a week later, the students who had written by hand understood the main ideas better. The researchers think this is because handwriting is slow, so students ( 1 ).

Typing, by contrast, allows students to copy down a lecture almost word for word. This might seem like an advantage, since they end up with more complete notes to study from. ( 2 ), the researchers found that students who typed often recorded information without really thinking about what it meant. Their notes were longer, but they remembered less of what they had heard. A similar pattern appeared in several later studies.

Not all experts agree with these conclusions, however. Some point out that laptops make it easy to organize, search, and share notes, which can be useful when reviewing for exams. Others suggest that the problem is not the device itself but the way it is used. If students using laptops are trained to summarize ideas in their own words instead of copying everything, they may ( 3 ). For now, the best advice may be for students to think carefully about how, and not just what, they write.

choices: can record every word the lecturer says
tend to lose interest in the lecture
must decide which information is most important
spend less time thinking about the topic
questions.why: 手書きは遅いので全部は書けない。だから何が大事かを選ぶ必要があり、理解が深まる。「すべての言葉を記録できる」はタイピングの方（第2段落）。

choices: In reality
Therefore
Similarly
In addition
questions.why: 前の文は「利点に思えるかもしれない」、後ろは「実は考えずに写していた」。見かけと実際の食い違いなので「実際には」。Therefore（だから）、Similarly（同様に）、In addition（さらに）は逆接にならない。

choices: no longer need to attend lectures
be unable to share their notes
gain the same benefits as those who write by hand
write much more slowly than before
questions.why: 問題は機器でなく使い方、という流れ。自分の言葉でまとめるよう訓練すれば、手書きと同じ効果が得られるかもしれない。講義に出なくてよい・共有できない、は本文と合わない。

sets.passage:
Quiet Cars, New Sounds

Electric cars are much quieter than cars with gasoline engines, especially at low speeds. For drivers, this is often seen as a benefit, as it makes driving in the city more relaxing. For people walking nearby, however, the silence can be a problem. Pedestrians who rely on sound to judge traffic, such as people with poor eyesight, may not notice an approaching electric car until it is very close. For this reason, several countries now ( 1 ).

Designing these sounds has turned out to be more complicated than expected. If a sound is too quiet, pedestrians will not hear it, but if it is too loud, it could add to noise pollution and annoy people living nearby. The sound also needs to change with speed so that pedestrians can tell whether a car is slowing down. Some car makers have hired composers and sound designers to create tones that are easy to notice yet pleasant to hear. ( 2 ), one company tested dozens of different sounds with volunteers before choosing a soft humming tone for its cars.

Interestingly, these sounds are also becoming a way for companies to ( 3 ). Just as people once recognized certain brands by the roar of their engines, some manufacturers hope customers will come to associate a particular tone with their cars. Critics worry that if every company chooses a different sound, streets could become confusing for pedestrians. Others, though, believe that a little variety is a small price to pay for safer roads.

choices: ban electric cars from busy city streets
require new electric cars to make an artificial sound at low speeds
encourage pedestrians to wear headphones
limit the number of electric cars sold each year
questions.why: 静かすぎて歩行者が気づかない、という問題への対策。次の段落が「これらの音を設計するのは難しい」と続くので、低速で人工の音を出させる決まり。

choices: Nonetheless
Otherwise
On the contrary
For instance
questions.why: 前の文は「作曲家を雇って心地よい音を作る」、後ろはある会社が何十もの音を試した具体例。だから「例えば」。Nonetheless（それでも）、Otherwise（さもないと）、On the contrary（それどころか）は合わない。

choices: reduce the price of their vehicles
make their cars travel faster
avoid following safety rules
give their products a distinctive identity
questions.why: かつてエンジン音でブランドが分かったように、特定の音を自社の車と結びつけてほしい、とある。だから「製品に独自の個性を持たせる」。値下げ・速さ・規則を避ける、は本文に無い。

sets.passage:
The Pull of Unfinished Tasks

Many people find that an unfinished task stays on their mind long after they have stopped working on it. A half-written report or an unanswered e-mail can keep coming back to their thoughts, even while they are trying to relax in the evening. For some, this can even make it hard to fall asleep. Psychologists have long observed that people tend to remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones. It seems that once a task is finished, the mind is able to ( 1 ).

This tendency can be stressful, but it can also be useful. Some writers deliberately stop working in the middle of a sentence at the end of each day. ( 2 ), they find it easier to start again the next morning, because they already know exactly what they want to say next. Teachers have used a similar idea by ending a lesson with an unanswered question, which encourages students to keep thinking about the topic until the following class.

For people who cannot stop thinking about work at night, however, researchers have suggested a simple solution. In one experiment, participants who wrote down a specific plan for completing their unfinished tasks were able to concentrate much better on a later activity than those who did not. They had not actually done any more work. It appears that the mind does not need a task to be finished in order to relax. Rather, it is enough to ( 3 ).

choices: remember it in even greater detail
stop treating it as something that needs attention
feel anxious about starting new work
lose interest in all other activities
questions.why: 途中の仕事は覚えている、と対比して「終わると」なので、もう気にかける必要がない物として扱う。「さらに詳しく覚える」は前の文と逆。

choices: By doing so
Even so
In contrast
Instead
questions.why: 前の文は「わざと文の途中で止める」、後ろはその結果「翌朝始めやすい」。手段とその効果なので「そうすることで」。Even so（それでも）、In contrast（対照的に）、Instead（その代わり）は合わない。

choices: forget about the task completely
complete several other tasks first
know when and how the task will be completed
ask someone else to finish the task
questions.why: 実験では、終わらせる具体的な計画を書いた人が集中できた。終わっていなくても「いつ・どうやって終えるか分かっていれば」十分。完全に忘れる、他人に頼む、は実験の内容と違う。

parts.intro: Read each passage and choose the best answer from the four choices for each question.

sets.passage:
The Value of Boredom

For many people today, a moment of boredom is something to be eliminated as quickly as possible. While waiting for a bus or standing in line at a store, most of us automatically reach for our smartphones to check messages, read the news, or play a game. Psychologists have noted that, as a result, many people now go through entire days without ever experiencing the feeling of having nothing to do. Although this might seem like a harmless habit, some researchers believe that constantly avoiding boredom may come at a cost.

In one common type of experiment, participants are first asked to complete a dull task, such as sorting a large pile of beans by color for fifteen minutes. Afterward, they are given a creative challenge, like thinking of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with participants who skipped the dull task, those who had been bored tend to produce a greater number of ideas, and their ideas are often judged to be more original. One explanation is that boredom encourages the mind to wander. When the brain is not occupied by outside information, it begins to make unexpected connections between memories and thoughts, a process that can lead to creative solutions.

Boredom may also play a role in motivating people to change their lives. Because the feeling is unpleasant, it signals that a person's current activity is not meaningful or rewarding enough. In this sense, boredom works much like hunger: it pushes us to search for something better. People who feel bored at work, for example, may be inspired to learn a new skill or look for a more challenging position. Researchers warn, however, that this benefit depends on how people respond. Those who react to boredom by turning to quick sources of entertainment, such as scrolling endlessly through social media, may relieve the feeling temporarily without ever addressing its cause.

None of this means that boredom is always good. Long periods of boredom, particularly among teenagers, have been linked with poor concentration and unhealthy habits. Nevertheless, some educators now argue that children should be given more unstructured time, free from screens and scheduled activities. Rather than rushing to fill every quiet moment, they suggest, parents and teachers could allow children to discover for themselves how to turn boredom into something productive. Learning to tolerate a little boredom, it seems, may be a valuable skill in a world full of constant distractions.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one finding of experiments on boredom?
choices: People who are easily bored find it difficult to complete simple tasks such as sorting beans.
Creative challenges become less interesting to people after they have used their smartphones.
People who have just performed a boring task often come up with more creative ideas.
People who avoid boredom are better at making connections between their memories.
questions.why: 第2段落：退屈な作業をした人のほうが、アイデアの数が多く独創的だった。豆の仕分けは実験の作業の例で、退屈しやすい人が苦手という話ではない。記憶をつなげるのは退屈した時の脳の働き。

questions.q: What does the author of the passage suggest about the way people respond to boredom?
choices: It is usually a sign that people are hungry or tired and need to take a rest.
People who feel bored at work should avoid changing their jobs too quickly.
Its benefits may be lost if people simply distract themselves with easy entertainment.
Using social media is an effective way to deal with the real cause of boredom.
questions.why: 第3段落の後半：SNS などすぐ手に入る娯楽に逃げると、一時的に気分は晴れても原因に向き合わない。hunger は「より良い物を探させる」たとえで、本当に空腹という意味ではない。

questions.q: Some educators believe that
choices: teenagers should spend longer periods alone in order to improve their concentration.
children may benefit from having free time without screens or planned activities.
schools should give children more structured activities to prevent them from feeling bored.
parents should fill their children's quiet moments with educational games.
questions.why: 第4段落：画面や予定の無い自由な時間を子どもに与えるべきだ、と主張する教育者がいる。長い退屈は10代の集中力低下と結びつくとあり、予定を詰める・静かな時間を埋める、は逆。

sets.passage:
Gardens on the Rooftops

In many cities around the world, rooftops are being transformed into gardens. These so-called green roofs are covered with a layer of soil and plants, ranging from simple grasses to small trees. Although the idea of growing plants on buildings is centuries old, it has attracted new attention as city governments search for ways to make urban areas more pleasant and environmentally friendly. In the city of Marston, for example, all new commercial buildings above a certain size must now include either a green roof or solar panels.

One major advantage of green roofs is their ability to manage rainwater. In ordinary cities, rain falls onto hard surfaces such as concrete and asphalt and flows rapidly into drains. During heavy rain, drainage systems can become overloaded, and water may collect on roads and sidewalks. A green roof, by contrast, absorbs much of the rain and releases it slowly over several hours. Some of the water is also taken up by the plants and returned to the air. Engineers in Marston estimate that the city's green roofs now hold back millions of liters of water each year that would otherwise have entered its crowded drains.

Green roofs can also help to cool both buildings and the surrounding area. Dark rooftops absorb heat from the sun, and in summer they can become hot enough to raise temperatures inside the building and in nearby streets. Plants, however, provide shade and release moisture, which keeps the roof surface much cooler. As a result, buildings with green roofs often need less air conditioning, which reduces energy costs. In addition, the gardens provide a home for insects and birds that would otherwise struggle to find food in the city.

Despite these benefits, green roofs are not suitable for every building. Soil soaked with water is extremely heavy, so older buildings may need to be strengthened before a roof garden can be added, which can be very expensive. Green roofs also require regular maintenance, such as removing weeds and checking that water is draining properly, and building owners are sometimes unwilling to pay for this. To encourage more people to install them, some cities offer financial support or reduce property taxes for owners who do so. Supporters believe that, as the costs of materials fall and more people become aware of the benefits, green roofs will become a common feature of city life.

questions.q: What is one way that green roofs help cities deal with rain?
choices: They slow down the speed at which rainwater reaches the drainage system.
They direct rainwater into large tanks so that it can later be used for drinking.
They prevent rain from ever falling onto concrete and asphalt surfaces.
They allow engineers to build smaller drains under the city's streets.
questions.why: 第2段落：雨を吸い込み、数時間かけてゆっくり放出する（releases it slowly）。だから排水管に一気に流れ込まない。飲み水のタンク・小さな排水管は本文に無い。

questions.q: According to the passage, green roofs can reduce energy costs because
choices: dark rooftops reflect the sun's heat away from the building.
the insects and birds living on the roof help to control temperatures.
they make it possible to install solar panels at a lower price.
the plants keep the roof cooler, so less air conditioning is needed.
questions.why: 第3段落：植物が日陰を作り水分を出すので屋根が涼しく、冷房が少なくて済む。黒い屋根は熱を吸収する（反射ではない）。鳥や虫は別の利点。

questions.q: What is one problem with installing green roofs?
choices: Cities have started to charge higher taxes to owners of buildings that have them.
Some buildings must be made stronger to support the weight of wet soil.
The plants used on green roofs often attract insects that damage buildings.
They cannot be combined with other systems such as solar panels.
questions.why: 第4段落：水を含んだ土はとても重く、古い建物は補強が必要で費用がかかる。税金はむしろ減らす市がある。太陽光パネルは「緑の屋根か太陽光パネル」の選択肢として出てくるだけ。

sets.passage:
Railways and the Birth of Standard Time

Today, it seems natural that everyone in the same region sets their clocks to the same time. For most of history, however, this was not the case. Before the nineteenth century, each town determined its own time based on the position of the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon arrived a few minutes earlier in a town in the east than in one slightly to the west. For people who rarely traveled far from home, these small differences did not matter at all.

The arrival of the railway changed this situation dramatically. Trains allowed people to travel long distances in just a few hours, and suddenly the variety of local times became a serious problem. A railway company operating across a large area had to publish timetables, but which town's time should those timetables follow? Some companies used the local time of the city where their headquarters were located, while others listed several different times for each station. Passengers often missed trains because they were confused about which time was being used. More seriously, the confusion made it difficult to schedule trains safely on shared tracks.

To solve this problem, railway companies began to adopt standard times that applied across entire regions. Instead of hundreds of local times, a country could be divided into a small number of time zones, each covering a wide area. Within a zone, every clock would show the same time, and neighboring zones would usually differ by exactly one hour. At first, this was simply a business decision by the railways, and many towns continued to use their own local time for everyday purposes. Some residents resented being told to follow "railway time," feeling that it was unnatural to ignore the sun.

Over time, however, the convenience of standard time won people over. As telegraph networks expanded, businesses and governments found it increasingly useful for everyone to agree on the time. Eventually, time zones were made official by law in many countries, and they were coordinated internationally so that the whole world could be connected by a single system. The next time you check the time on your phone, it may be worth remembering that the familiar idea of a shared time was, in large part, created by the needs of the railways.

questions.q: Before the nineteenth century,
choices: each town set its clocks according to where the sun was.
towns in the east set their clocks later than towns in the west.
most people traveled long distances in order to compare local times.
noon was decided by a national organization in each country.
questions.why: 第1段落：町ごとに太陽の位置で時刻を決め、太陽が一番高い時が正午。東の町のほうが正午が早く来る（later ではない）。遠出する人は少なかった。

questions.q: What problem did railway companies face?
choices: Passengers refused to buy tickets unless timetables used their own local time.
Their headquarters were located too far from most of the stations they served.
Trains could not travel quickly enough to make long journeys practical.
The many different local times made it hard to create clear and safe schedules.
questions.why: 第2段落：どの町の時刻で時刻表を作るか決められず、乗客は混乱し、同じ線路での安全な運行も難しかった。本社の時刻を使った会社はあるが、距離が問題だったわけではない。

questions.q: What does the passage say about the introduction of standard time?
choices: It was not immediately accepted by everyone, but its usefulness gradually became clear.
It was first introduced by law and was later adopted by the railway companies.
Neighboring time zones were set several hours apart in order to avoid confusion.
Telegraph companies opposed it because it made their services less necessary.
questions.why: 第3・4段落：初めは反発する住民もいたが、電信の広がりとともに便利さが認められた。順番は鉄道会社が先で法律は後。隣の時間帯の差はふつう1時間。

sets.passage:
Learning from the Bottom Up

In most companies, mentoring follows a familiar pattern: an experienced senior employee offers advice and guidance to a younger colleague who is just beginning his or her career. In recent years, however, a growing number of organizations have started to experiment with the opposite arrangement. In so-called reverse mentoring programs, junior employees are paired with senior managers, and it is the younger employee who acts as the teacher.

The idea first became popular as a way to help senior staff keep up with new technology. Many executives built their careers before social media and smartphone apps became central to business, and some feel uncomfortable using them. A young employee who has grown up with these tools can explain not only how they work but also how customers of his or her generation actually use them. At Brightwell Insurance, a mid-sized firm, managers who took part in such a program said they had gained a far better understanding of why the company's online advertising was failing to reach younger customers.

Supporters argue, however, that the benefits go well beyond technical skills. In many organizations, junior employees rarely have the chance to speak directly with top managers, and their opinions may pass through several layers of supervisors before reaching the people who make decisions. Reverse mentoring creates a direct channel of communication. Senior managers can learn what younger staff think about issues such as working conditions and company culture, while junior employees gain confidence and a clearer view of how the business is run. Some companies have also found that employees who participate are less likely to quit, which can save considerable recruitment costs.

Nevertheless, reverse mentoring programs do not always succeed. Some senior managers find it difficult to accept advice from people much younger than themselves, and they may not take the sessions seriously. Junior employees, for their part, may hesitate to give honest feedback to someone who has power over their careers. Experts recommend that companies set clear goals for each pair and make it explicit that the sessions are confidential. They also suggest that the mentoring should go both ways, with each person sharing knowledge with the other. When these conditions are met, reverse mentoring can help to break down the barriers between generations in the workplace.

questions.q: Why did reverse mentoring first become popular?
choices: It allowed companies to train new employees without hiring outside experts.
Senior managers wanted to teach younger staff how to use social media for business.
Younger employees demanded more opportunities to be promoted to senior positions.
It offered a way for senior staff to learn about new technology from younger colleagues.
questions.why: 第2段落：上の世代が新しい技術についていくための方法として広まった。教えるのは若い社員の側なので、上司が SNS を教える、は逆。

questions.q: According to supporters, one benefit of reverse mentoring is that
choices: it reduces the number of supervisors that a company needs to employ.
it allows the opinions of junior staff to reach senior managers more directly.
it gives senior managers a chance to criticize younger employees' work.
it makes it easier for companies to recruit staff from other firms.
questions.why: 第3段落：若手の意見は何層もの上司を通るが、この制度は直接の連絡の道を作る。採用費が減るのは辞める人が減るからで、他社から人を取りやすくなるわけではない。

questions.q: What do experts recommend in order to make reverse mentoring programs successful?
choices: Allowing senior managers to choose which junior employees they work with.
Recording each session so that supervisors can check what was discussed.
Making sure that both people in each pair learn something from each other.
Limiting the program to employees who have worked at the company for many years.
questions.why: 第4段落：目標をはっきりさせ、内容は秘密にし、お互いに教え合う（go both ways）ようにする。秘密にするので、記録して上司が確認する、は逆。

sets.passage:
The First Self-Service Stores

Before the twentieth century, shopping for groceries usually meant standing at a counter and asking a clerk for each item. The clerk would collect the goods from shelves behind the counter, weigh them, and wrap them, while other customers waited their turn. This system gave store owners a great deal of control over what customers bought, but it was slow and required many employees. In busy neighborhoods, shoppers sometimes spent more time waiting in line than actually shopping. Clerks also had to remember the prices of hundreds of items, and mistakes in calculating bills were common.

In the early 1900s, some store owners began experimenting with a new idea: allowing customers to walk through the store and pick up products themselves. At first, many people in the industry were doubtful. They worried that customers would be confused without a clerk's help and that goods would be damaged or put back in the wrong places. To deal with these concerns, early self-service stores were often designed with a single path that led shoppers past every shelf and ended at a checkout counter near the exit. Shoppers were also given baskets, an idea that seems obvious today but was considered new at the time.

The new system turned out to have advantages that its inventors had not fully expected. Because fewer clerks were needed, stores could lower their prices, which attracted more customers. More importantly, shoppers who could see and touch products often bought items they had not planned to buy. Store owners began placing popular products in certain locations to encourage this. Manufacturers quickly realized that the appearance of a product's package now mattered a great deal, since it had to catch the eye of shoppers without a clerk recommending it. This led to a boom in colorful packaging and brand advertising.

Today, self-service is so common that it is hard to imagine shopping any other way. However, some observers note that the original trade-offs remain. While customers enjoy lower prices and greater freedom, they have also lost the personal advice that clerks once provided. Many shoppers find it hard to choose between dozens of similar products without help. Some small grocery stores have begun to attract customers by offering exactly this kind of service, hiring knowledgeable staff who can recommend ingredients and explain how to cook them. For these stores, the human touch that self-service removed has become a selling point.

questions.q: According to the passage, what was one problem with the traditional way of shopping for groceries?
choices: It took a long time and needed a large number of workers.
Customers were allowed to take products from any shelf.
Store owners could not decide which goods to sell.
Clerks often recommended products that were too expensive.
questions.why: 第1段落：店員が一つずつ取って量り包むので遅く、多くの従業員が必要だった。棚から自由に取るのはセルフサービスの方。

questions.q: Why did package design become more important after self-service stores appeared?
choices: Stores required manufacturers to make their packages smaller.
Clerks refused to recommend products in plain packages.
Products needed to attract shoppers' attention without help from a clerk.
Customers preferred to buy goods that had been wrapped by hand.
questions.why: 第3段落：店員が勧めてくれないので、包装そのものが客の目を引く必要があった。包装を小さく、手で包んだ物を好む、は本文に無い。

questions.q: What do some small grocery stores do today?
choices: They have stopped allowing customers to choose products themselves.
They attract customers by providing the kind of personal advice that self-service removed.
They offer lower prices than large supermarkets by hiring fewer staff.
They require customers to follow a single path through the store.
questions.why: 第4段落：詳しい店員を雇い、材料や料理法を勧める。セルフサービスで失われた人の助言を売りにしている。一本道の通路は初期の店の話。

sets.passage:
City Birds Change Their Tune

For birds, singing is not simply a pleasant activity. Males of many species sing to attract partners and to warn rivals to stay out of their territory. For these messages to work, however, they must be heard clearly. In cities, this has become increasingly difficult, as the constant low-pitched noise of traffic and construction can drown out birdsong. A song that cannot be heard by a female or a rival is of little use. As cities grow, more and more birds face this problem every day.

Researchers studying songbirds in several large cities have found that some species have responded by changing the way they sing. Birds living near busy roads tend to sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species living in quiet forests. Because traffic noise is mostly low-pitched, higher notes are less likely to be covered up. Some urban birds have also started singing earlier in the morning, before rush hour begins, or singing more loudly than their relatives in the countryside. In quieter parts of the same city, however, birds of the same species often sing lower songs, much like their relatives in forests.

These changes may help birds communicate, but they could also have costs. In some species, females seem to prefer males that sing lower songs, possibly because low notes are a sign of a larger, healthier bird. A male that raises the pitch of his song to be heard over traffic may therefore become less attractive. Singing more loudly also requires more energy, which could leave birds with less strength for finding food. Birds that start singing very early may also lose valuable time for rest. Scientists are still trying to determine whether city birds raise as many young as those in quieter areas.

The research has encouraged some cities to look for ways to reduce noise in parks and green spaces. Planting thick rows of trees and bushes along roads, for example, can absorb some traffic sound. Road surfaces made of special materials can also reduce the noise from tires. In one city, a trial that lowered speed limits on the roads next to a large park led to a noticeable drop in noise levels, and researchers later recorded more bird species singing there. Such findings suggest that making cities quieter could benefit not only people but also the wildlife that shares their neighborhoods.

questions.q: Why do some birds in cities sing at a higher pitch?
choices: Females in cities prefer males with high voices.
They are smaller than birds that live in forests.
They need to warn other birds about approaching cars.
Higher sounds are less likely to be hidden by traffic noise.
questions.why: 第2段落：交通の騒音は主に低い音なので、高い音の方がかき消されにくい。メスはむしろ低い歌を好む（第3段落）。

questions.q: What is one possible problem with the changes in city birds' songs?
choices: Females may find males with higher songs less appealing.
Birds that sing early cannot find enough food in the morning.
The new songs can no longer be heard by other members of the species.
The birds are no longer able to defend their territory.
questions.why: 第3段落：低い歌は大きく健康なしるしなので、高く歌うオスは魅力が下がるかもしれない。大きな声はエネルギーを使うとあるが、朝食べ物が見つからないとは言っていない。

questions.q: What happened when speed limits were lowered near a park?
choices: Drivers began using other roads that passed through the park.
Fewer trees and bushes were needed along the roads.
Residents complained that traffic jams had become worse.
The area became quieter, and more kinds of birds were heard singing.
questions.why: 第4段落：騒音がはっきり下がり、後で歌う鳥の種類が増えた。木の列は別の対策の例で、減らしたわけではない。

sets.passage:
Science by the Public

Scientific research is usually thought of as the work of professionals in laboratories. In recent decades, however, millions of ordinary people have taken part in what is known as citizen science. Volunteers count birds in their gardens, record the dates when local flowers bloom, or use smartphone apps to photograph insects. The information they collect is then sent to researchers, who use it in their studies. Some projects involve only a few hundred people, while others have attracted hundreds of thousands of volunteers from many countries.

The biggest advantage of citizen science is scale. A small team of scientists can only be in a few places at once, but thousands of volunteers can gather observations across an entire country. One long-running project asks people to report the first day each spring that they see certain kinds of butterflies. By comparing reports from many years, researchers have been able to show that several species now appear earlier than they did a few decades ago, a change that would have been almost impossible to detect without so many observers. Professional researchers simply could not afford to employ enough people to collect such information.

Critics have raised concerns about the quality of the data, however. Volunteers may misidentify species or forget to report days when they saw nothing at all, which can make results unreliable. Some volunteers may also report only unusual sightings, since common species seem less interesting to record. To address this problem, many projects now provide online training and ask volunteers to upload photographs so that experts can check difficult identifications. Researchers have also developed statistical methods that can account for common mistakes. Studies comparing volunteer data with data collected by professionals have generally found that, when such checks are in place, the two are surprisingly similar.

Citizen science also benefits the volunteers themselves. Surveys of participants show that many become more interested in science and more aware of environmental issues after joining a project. Some even change their own behavior, for example by planting flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Some teachers have begun including citizen science activities in their lessons, finding that students are more motivated when they know their observations will be used by real researchers. For many participants, the knowledge that they are contributing to scientific discoveries is a reward in itself.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is the main advantage of citizen science?
choices: It is cheaper because volunteers buy their own equipment.
Volunteers are better at identifying butterflies than scientists are.
It allows information to be collected over a much wider area.
It allows researchers to stop working in laboratories.
questions.why: 第2段落：最大の利点は規模。少人数の科学者には無理な、国全体の観察が集まる。費用や、科学者より上手、は本文に無い。

questions.q: How have projects tried to improve the quality of volunteers' data?
choices: By only accepting reports from professional scientists.
By training volunteers and having experts check their photographs.
By asking volunteers to report only on days when they see something.
By reducing the number of volunteers in each project.
questions.why: 第3段落：オンライン研修と、写真を上げて専門家が確認する仕組み。「何も見なかった日を報告し忘れる」のが問題なので、見た日だけ報告させる、は逆。

questions.q: What have some teachers found?
choices: Students try harder when they know researchers will use their observations.
Students prefer studying science in laboratories to doing outdoor activities.
Citizen science projects are too difficult for most students.
Students become less interested in environmental issues after joining projects.
questions.why: 第4段落：本物の研究者が観察を使うと分かると、生徒のやる気が上がる。環境への関心はむしろ高まる。

sets.passage:
Following the Footsteps

In almost any park or university campus, there are narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass. These informal trails, sometimes called desire paths, appear when many people choose a route that is shorter or more convenient than the paved paths provided. Over time, their footsteps wear away the grass, leaving a visible line that shows how people actually prefer to move from one place to another. Such paths can be found almost anywhere people walk regularly, from city parks to the areas around train stations.

For a long time, landscape designers and building managers viewed desire paths as a problem. They put up fences, planted bushes, or added signs asking people to stay on the paths. Some even placed large rocks along the edges of lawns. Such efforts were often unsuccessful, however. People tended to walk around the fences or simply ignored the signs, and new trails soon appeared next to the old ones. Some managers spent large amounts of money repairing lawns, only to see them worn down again within months.

More recently, some planners have begun to treat desire paths as useful information. One university, when building a new campus, decided not to lay any paths at all during the first year. Instead, it planted grass everywhere and waited to see where students and staff walked. After a year, the worn trails clearly showed the most popular routes between buildings, and the university paved them. Because the paths matched how people actually moved, few new trails appeared afterward. The university also saved money that it would otherwise have spent on repairing damaged grass, and some students enjoyed the idea that they had helped design their campus.

The idea behind this approach has spread beyond the design of parks. Some software designers, for example, study how people actually use an app rather than how they were expected to use it, and then make the most common actions easier. If many users take an unexpected route to reach a certain feature, designers may move that feature to where people look for it. Supporters say the lesson is that designs work best when they follow people's habits instead of trying to control them. Others warn, though, that the shortest route is not always the best one, especially when a path would damage a sensitive area such as a riverbank or a field of rare plants.

questions.q: How did managers traditionally respond to desire paths?
choices: They paved the trails as soon as they appeared.
They asked students to help design new paths.
They tried to keep people off the grass, often without success.
They moved buildings closer together to shorten routes.
questions.why: 第2段落：柵・植え込み・看板で道から外れさせないようにしたが、うまくいかないことが多かった。踏み跡を舗装したのは最近の大学の例。

questions.q: What did one university do when building a new campus?
choices: It put up fences to protect the grass during the first year.
It asked designers to plan the shortest routes between buildings.
It repaired the lawn every few months after students damaged it.
It waited to see where people walked before deciding where to put paths.
questions.why: 第3段落：1年間は道を作らず、人が歩いた跡を見てから舗装した。柵で守る・数か月ごとに芝を直す、は昔のやり方。

questions.q: What is one concern about following people's habits in design?
choices: Software may become too difficult for people to use.
The most direct route may harm places that need protection.
People may stop using paths once they are paved.
Designers may no longer be needed in the future.
questions.why: 第4段落の最後：一番近い道が最善とは限らず、川岸や珍しい植物の野原を傷めることがある。ソフトはむしろ使いやすくなる例。
